_link.title: I can describe how the rate of a reaction can be monitored by measuring changes in gas volume or mass over time

toLevel2.stem: If a reaction produces a gas, what can be measured over time to monitor the rate?
distractors: The colour of the gas produced
The temperature of the gas only
The density of the solid reactant

toLevel2.stem: In an open system where gas escapes, what measurement can indicate reaction rate?
toLevel2.answer: The decrease in mass of the flask over time
distractors: The increase in mass of the flask over time
The temperature of the surrounding air
The colour change of the solution only

toLevel2.stem: Why might gas volume or mass loss be used instead of concentration to monitor rate?
toLevel2.answer: They are often easier to measure with standard lab equipment
distractors: Concentration always gives incorrect rate values
Gas volume is the only valid measure of rate
Mass loss is always more accurate than concentration

toLevel2.stem: In the reaction of CaCO₃ with HCl, which gas is produced and can be used to monitor rate?
distractors: Oxygen
Hydrogen
Nitrogen

toLevel2.stem: When monitoring rate by collecting gas, a gas syringe or inverted measuring cylinder is typically used to measure:
distractors: the mass of gas produced
the pressure of gas produced
the temperature of gas produced

toLevel2.stem: The rate of a gas-producing reaction can be monitored by measuring the volume of gas collected over time.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: Mass loss can only be used to monitor rate in a closed system where no gas can escape.
distractors: True

toLevel2.stem: If a reaction produces a gas, the {{blank:1}} of gas collected can be measured over {{blank:2}} to determine the rate.
distractors: colour
distance
density
mass

toLevel2.stem: In an open system, the {{blank:1}} of the flask decreases as {{blank:2}} escapes during the reaction.
distractors: volume
liquid
temperature
heat

toLevel2.stem: When CaCO₃ reacts with HCl, {{blank:1}} gas is produced, and a balance can record the {{blank:2}} in mass over time.
distractors: O₂
increase
H₂
change

toLevel3.stem: Why does the mass of a flask decrease during a gas-producing reaction in an open system?
toLevel3.answer: The gas produced escapes into the atmosphere, reducing the total mass
distractors: The reactants become lighter as they undergo a chemical change
The balance becomes less accurate as the reaction proceeds
The flask itself loses mass due to the heat of the reaction

toLevel3.stem: Why is gas volume collection only suitable for reactions that produce a gas?
toLevel3.answer: If no gas is produced, there is nothing to collect in a syringe or cylinder
distractors: Gas volume collection works for all types of reactions equally well
Liquids can also be collected in a gas syringe during a reaction
Gas volume is a universal measure that applies to any chemical change

toLevel3.stem: On a volume-time graph for a gas-producing reaction, a steeper initial curve indicates:
toLevel3.answer: a faster initial rate of reaction
distractors: a slower initial rate of reaction
a higher activation energy for the reaction
a greater total amount of gas will be produced

toLevel3.stem: On a mass-time graph for an open-system gas-producing reaction, the mass decreases and then levels off. Why does it level off?
toLevel3.answer: The reaction is nearing completion and gas production has slowed or stopped
distractors: The gas is being reabsorbed by the solution as the reaction proceeds
The balance has reached its minimum reading and cannot go lower
The flask is sealed and preventing further gas from escaping

toLevel3.stem: Why is measuring mass loss sometimes preferred over gas volume collection?
toLevel3.answer: Mass loss requires only a balance, which is simpler to set up than gas collection apparatus
distractors: Mass loss always gives more accurate results than gas volume collection
Gas volume collection cannot be done in a school laboratory setting
Mass loss measures concentration directly while gas volume does not

toLevel3.stem: Why would mass loss be an unreliable measure of rate if the gas produced is very light, like hydrogen?
toLevel3.answer: The mass change may be too small for a standard balance to detect accurately
distractors: Light gases cannot escape from an open flask under any conditions
Hydrogen gas increases the mass of the flask instead of decreasing it
Light gases do not count as products in a chemical reaction

toLevel3.stem: A steeper slope on a volume-time graph for gas collection indicates a faster rate of reaction.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: The mass of a flask decreases during a gas-producing reaction in an open system because gas {{blank:1}} into the atmosphere, reducing the total {{blank:2}}.
distractors: dissolves
volume
condenses
pressure

toLevel3.stem: A volume-time graph levels off when the reaction is nearing {{blank:1}} and gas {{blank:2}} has slowed or stopped.
distractors: equilibrium
absorption
beginning
compression

toLevel3.stem: Mass loss may be unreliable for very {{blank:1}} gases like H₂ because the change is too {{blank:2}} for a standard balance to detect.
distractors: heavy
large
dense
rapid

toLevel4.stem: A student reacts magnesium with hydrochloric acid in an open flask on a balance. They record the mass every 30 seconds. What trend should they observe?
toLevel4.answer: Mass decreases over time as hydrogen gas escapes
distractors: Mass increases over time as products are formed
Mass stays constant because the system is open
Mass decreases then increases as the reaction reverses

toLevel4.stem: A student collects gas using an inverted measuring cylinder during a reaction. After 120 seconds, 48 mL of gas has been collected. What is the average rate of gas production?
distractors: 4.0 mL s⁻¹
48 mL s⁻¹
0.04 mL s⁻¹

toLevel4.stem: A student wants to compare the rates of two gas-producing reactions. They collect gas from each using identical syringes. Which feature of the volume-time graphs should they compare?
toLevel4.answer: The steepness of the curves at corresponding time points
distractors: The colour of the gas collected in each syringe
The total mass of the gas syringes at the end
The temperature of the gas inside each syringe

toLevel4.stem: A student records mass loss data: 150.0 g at t=0, 149.2 g at t=60 s, 148.8 g at t=120 s. In which time interval was the rate faster?
toLevel4.answer: The first 60 seconds, with 0.8 g lost compared to 0.4 g in the second interval
distractors: The second 60 seconds, with 0.4 g lost compared to 0.8 g in the first
Both intervals had the same rate because the time interval was equal
The rate cannot be compared from mass loss data alone

toLevel4.stem: A student investigates the effect of temperature on rate by reacting CaCO₃ with HCl at two temperatures and collecting CO₂ gas. What should they plot?
toLevel4.answer: Volume of CO₂ collected versus time for each temperature
distractors: Temperature versus concentration for each trial
Mass of CaCO₃ versus volume of HCl for each trial
Activation energy versus temperature on one graph

toLevel4.stem: A student uses a cotton wool plug in the top of a flask to prevent liquid splashing out while still allowing gas to escape for mass loss measurement. Why is this better than leaving the flask completely open?
toLevel4.answer: It prevents loss of liquid spray while still allowing gas to escape for accurate mass readings
distractors: It seals the flask completely to create a closed system for the experiment
It absorbs the gas produced so that mass loss cannot be measured
It increases the rate of reaction by compressing the gas inside the flask

toLevel4.stem: A student collects hydrogen gas from a reaction using a gas syringe. After 5 minutes, the syringe stops moving. What does this indicate?
toLevel4.answer: The reaction has reached completion and no more gas is being produced
distractors: The syringe has broken and can no longer collect gas
The reaction has reversed and is consuming the hydrogen
The temperature has dropped to zero stopping all gas production

toLevel4.stem: A student records 48 mL of gas collected in 120 seconds. The average rate of gas production is {{blank:1}} mL s⁻¹, calculated by dividing {{blank:2}} by time.
distractors: mass
pressure

toLevel4.stem: A cotton wool plug allows {{blank:1}} to escape for mass measurement while preventing {{blank:2}} from splashing out.
distractors: liquid
gas
heat
solid

toLevel4.stem: When a gas syringe stops moving during gas collection, it indicates the reaction has reached {{blank:1}} and no more {{blank:2}} is being produced.
distractors: equilibrium
heat
maximum
liquid

toLevel5.stem: A student measures both gas volume collected and mass loss for the same reaction simultaneously. They find the mass loss data is less smooth. What might explain this?
toLevel5.answer: Small fluctuations in balance readings and air currents can affect mass measurements more than gas syringe readings
distractors: Mass loss is always more accurate than gas volume collection in every case
Gas volume and mass loss should always give identical, perfectly smooth data
The gas syringe is affected by air currents but the balance is not

toLevel5.stem: A student argues: 'Gas volume collection is always better than mass loss for monitoring rate.' Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: Not always — mass loss is simpler to set up and may be preferred when precise gas collection is difficult
distractors: Correct — gas volume is always more accurate than mass loss in every case
Incorrect — mass loss is always superior to gas volume for monitoring rate
Correct — mass loss cannot be used in any situation to measure reaction rate

toLevel5.stem: Two students monitor the same CaCO₃ + HCl reaction. Student A measures gas volume; Student B measures mass loss. Both calculate rate. How should their calculated rates relate?
toLevel5.answer: They should show the same trend, but the numerical values will differ because the units are different
distractors: Both should get identical numerical values for rate at every point
Student A's values will always be exactly twice Student B's values
The two methods cannot measure the same reaction simultaneously

toLevel5.stem: A student measures mass loss for a reaction that produces a very soluble gas (like HCl gas). Why might this be problematic?
toLevel5.answer: The soluble gas may dissolve in the solution instead of escaping, giving inaccurate mass loss readings
distractors: Soluble gases always escape faster than insoluble gases from open flasks
Soluble gases increase the mass of the flask rather than decreasing it
There is no problem because all gases behave identically in mass loss experiments

toLevel5.stem: A volume-time graph shows gas being produced rapidly at first, then the rate gradually slows. A mass-time graph for the same reaction shows mass decreasing rapidly at first, then levelling off. Why do both graphs show the same pattern?
toLevel5.answer: Both are measuring the same reaction — as reactants are consumed, the rate slows and eventually stops
distractors: The graphs show different patterns because they measure different things
The volume graph should show a constant rate throughout the reaction
The mass graph should show mass increasing as products are formed

toLevel5.stem: A student is designing an experiment to measure the rate of a reaction producing oxygen gas. They can choose gas collection or mass loss. The expected total gas production is only 5 mL. Which method is better?
toLevel5.answer: Gas collection — the mass change from 5 mL of O₂ would be too small for most balances to detect
distractors: Mass loss — because it is always more accurate than gas collection
Either method would work equally well for such a small gas volume
Mass loss — because balances can detect any mass change no matter how small

toLevel5.stem: A student uses gas collection to measure rate and notices the gas syringe moves in small jumps rather than smoothly. What might explain this?
toLevel5.answer: Gas is produced in bursts as bubbles form and release from the solid surface intermittently
distractors: The gas syringe is broken and needs to be replaced immediately
The reaction has stopped and restarted multiple times during the experiment
The temperature is fluctuating wildly causing intermittent gas production

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that measuring gas volume in a closed system using a pressure sensor is more accurate than using a gas syringe in an open system. Under what condition is this valid?
toLevel5.answer: When precise, continuous data is needed and the closed system prevents gas loss
distractors: Pressure sensors are always less accurate than gas syringes in all situations
Closed systems cannot be used to measure the rate of any gas-producing reaction
Gas syringes are always more accurate because they measure volume directly

toLevel5.stem: Both volume-time and mass-time graphs show the same overall {{blank:1}} because both methods are measuring the same {{blank:2}} proceeding at the same rate.
distractors: values
gas
units
product

toLevel5.stem: For reactions producing very small amounts of gas, {{blank:1}} collection is preferred over mass loss because the mass change may be too {{blank:2}} to detect accurately.
distractors: mass
large
volume
rapid
